# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Transitions

There's a moment I think about often—probably too often—that happened on an ordinary Tuesday morning last spring. I was sitting in a coffee shop, the kind that's trying very hard to be a specific aesthetic of "cozy urban sophistication," all Edison bulbs and reclaimed wood and a barista who knew everyone's name. I wasn't particularly happy or sad. I wasn't waiting for anything important. But I became suddenly, intensely aware that I was alive, that this moment was happening, that the woman next to me was reading a book with a cracked spine, and that the light was hitting the table at an angle that made the coffee ripple slightly when someone walked past.

This awareness lasted maybe forty-five seconds. Then it was gone, swallowed back into the normal current of consciousness. But it left me thinking: why do we have these moments? What are they for?

I think they might be for nothing. That might be the point.

We're so accustomed to assigning utility to everything—to asking "what's the point?" until we've miniaturized all of life into a series of productivity metrics and goal-completion markers—that we've almost forgotten there's another category of human experience. The experiences that don't lead anywhere. The moments that don't accumulate toward something else. Just moments, in themselves, complete and sufficient.

The coffee shop moment came back to me because I was reading about a concept in Buddhism called "suchness"—the idea that things are simply as they are, and that seeing them clearly without layering interpretations on top is a kind of enlightenment. Not a dramatic enlightenment with flashing lights and spiritual trumpets, but a quiet one. The enlightenment of noticing that the cup is a cup, the table is a table, the morning light is just morning light, and that this is already enough.

I've been thinking a lot lately about transitions, too. We treat them as problems to be solved—moving from one place to another, one job to another, one phase of life to another. We have advice columns and self-help books and therapists all dedicated to "managing" transitions, as though they're something to be gotten through efficiently so we can arrive at the next stable state. But what if transitions are actually where the interesting stuff lives?

Think about spring, which I've been experiencing with unusual attention this year. Everyone talks about spring as though it's a destination, a state to be achieved: spring is here, spring has sprung, spring is in full bloom. But spring itself is not a stable state at all. Spring is pure transition. Every day in spring is literally different from the last one—there's something new in bloom, something else is changing. If you try to capture spring as a state, you miss it. The only way to actually experience spring is to be aware of the constant, gentle flux. The same tree blooms a little more each day. The same grass grows a little taller. The same birds' chorus gets a little louder and more complex.

A friend of mine is between jobs right now. She's been calling this her "liminal period," with a sort of self-aware irony, but I think she's onto something real. She has flexible days now. She wakes up and doesn't immediately know what the day requires of her. This is making her anxious because we're all raised to believe that unstructured time is failure-time, wasted-time, the time in which you're not becoming whoever you're supposed to become. But what she's discovered, almost by accident, is that the unstructured time is when she actually thinks. When she wonders about things. When she reads books just because they interest her. When she sits in parks and watches people without any particular purpose.

She'll get a new job eventually. The structured time will return. And some of what she's enjoying will be displaced by the obligations that come with being employed. I don't think that's tragic, exactly—we need structure, and structure itself isn't bad. But I do think there's something worth noticing about how we treat the gaps between structures as though they're just dead time, waiting time, rather than recognizing that gaps might be their own kind of existence.

I've been reading a lot of poetry lately, which is a thing I do when I'm unsettled without quite knowing why. Poetry is the genre most interested in the spaces between things—between words, between meaning and sound, between what's said and what's implied. Poetry loves transitions. It's almost all transitions. A good poem is basically a series of small philosophical collisions, moments where one image or idea bumps up against another and something sparks in the space between them.

There's a poem by Mary Oliver where she asks, "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" It's become so iconic that it's almost been drained of power—it's on posters and Instagram graphics and corporate wellness slides. But reading it actually, in context, it's a different thing. It's not a demand that you be impressive or productive. It's a genuine question. What are you going to do with it? 

And I think the honest answer, for most people, most of the time, is: I'm going to live it. I'm going to have moments and conversations and breakfasts and small insights and frustrations and boring Tuesday afternoons and occasional flashes of beauty and long stretches where nothing much happens. I'm going to exist in time, move through it, watch it change around me. And that's already quite a lot.

There's this thing that happens in conversations where someone says something true and everyone stops talking for a second, not an awkward silence but a real one, a silence with weight in it. Those moments feel important to me. They feel like windows into how we actually are with each other when we're not performing. They're not lasting. They're not productive. But they matter.

I've become fascinated by the idea that some of the most important things in life might be the ones that don't "matter" in any measurable sense. A conversation that changes your perspective but doesn't change your job or your status. A book that reshapes how you think but doesn't advance your career. A friendship that nourishes you but exists mostly in quiet moments with no story to tell about it afterward. A walk where nothing happens except that you see some trees and sky and feel your own existence for a while.

The productivity culture we live in is so loudly insistent that these things should be optimized—that even rest should be "restorative," even hobbies should build toward something, even relationships should "bring value" to your life. And I'm not immune to this. I notice that even my thinking about the value of unstructured time is partly an attempt to justify it in terms that our culture will recognize as valid. See, I'm saying, the unstructured time is actually valuable because it develops your thinking and makes you more creative and resilient. So it counts.

But what if some things don't count? What if they don't need to count? What if the point of breakfast is just breakfast—the taste of it, the company possibly, the simple fact of fuel and nourishment and a moment in the day? What if the point of a walk is just the walking?

I think about death sometimes—not in a morbid way, but as a practical reality that shapes everything. We're all practicing dying, in a way. Every moment that passes is a moment we won't get back. Every day we're a little closer to the end. This could be depressing information, and it can be, but it can also be clarifying. It makes some things seem more important and other things seem less important. All those accumulated achievements and status markers—they're real, they matter in their way, but they also don't matter at all in the face of the actual, lived experience of being alive.

My therapist (yes, I have one, and yes, this is relevant) once said something that stuck with me. She said that a lot of suffering comes from the gap between how we think life should be and how it actually is. Life should be productive and meaningful and leading somewhere. Life should fit into a narrative with a clear arc. Life should make sense. But actual life is mostly just... life. Mundane, repetitive, sideways, full of things that don't lead anywhere. And the suffering isn't in the mundanity—it's in wanting it to be otherwise.

I've been trying to practice noticing things as they are. Not as they should be, not as they might lead to, not as they mean or represent. Just as they are. The coffee tastes like coffee. The morning is morning. The person across from me on the train is just a person existing in their own interior world that I'll never have access to. This should be obvious, but I find it genuinely difficult.

There's something about being human in 2024—whenever you're reading this, though probably some version of this is always true—that makes us resistant to just existing. We're always evaluating, always narrating, always trying to extract meaning or productivity or validation from every moment. We're performing our lives as much as living them. We're curating our own experience as it happens, imagining how we'll tell it to someone else, how it will look when we've turned it into a story.

I wonder what it would be like to just stop. To have a day where you don't narrate it, don't evaluate it, don't try to make it meaningful or productive or share-worthy. Just have the day. Just be in it. I've never quite managed it, but I think that might be close to what people mean by peace.

There's a Japanese concept—I'm probably butchering this—of "ma," which refers to the space between things, the emptiness that makes the things meaningful. In music, it's the silence between notes. In design, it's the white space. In conversation, it's the pause. The idea is that what we usually think of as the "content" is only meaningful because of the empty space around it. Take away all the silence, all the space, and you don't get more music, you get noise.

I think a life is like that too. We think the meaningful stuff is the achievements, the relationships, the accumulation of experiences and credentials and stories. But maybe the meaningful stuff is actually the spaces between—the quiet moments, the fallow periods, the transitions, the waiting, the ordinary days. These aren't gaps that need to be filled. They're the structure that allows everything else to have shape.

I don't know if I believe this entirely. I have ambitions and goals and things I want to accomplish, and I think those matter. I'm not trying to argue for the complete surrender to passivity. But I do think we've gotten the proportion wrong. We've made the ma into the thing and the thing into the ma. We've made the spaces between matter less than the peaks. And I think if we could somehow recalibrate—not giving up on meaning or productivity or direction, but just getting the volume right on all the in-between moments—we might find that life is already here, already happening, already enough.

That Tuesday in the coffee shop, when I suddenly noticed that I was alive—I think that was the point of that day. Not that something happened on that day, not that it led somewhere, not that I learned something I could make productive use of. The point was just: I was alive, light was hitting a table, someone was reading, and for a moment I noticed. That was the whole thing. That was enough.
